beats.narration_text: Nihao — this is Liam, in for Bear. Someone drops a model comparison table. The premium model wins most rows. It costs twice as much. The cheaper one loses the headline benchmark but costs half. Before you decide what to buy, this episode is a field guide: how to read that table without getting played.

props.command: A comparison table shows the premium model winning most rows at twice the price. Which model do we buy?
props.runningText: reading the table without getting played…
output: Five traps sit between you and an honest read of that table
The headline isn't pure — the score wraps a system — the effort's unmatched
And the price on the label is not the cost you'll pay

beats.act: ACT I — The Table Wants to Fool You
beats.narration_text: Act one. The table wants to fool you — specifically.

lines: The Table Wants to Fool You

beats.narration_text: Here is the table. A pen circles the winning rows. The premium model wins five, ties one, loses three. Count the wins — that's the temptation. The table is staging a naïve read for you.

manim.spec: drawn comparison table two columns (PREMIUM/CHEAPER); 9 task rows W/L/T; terracotta circles animate onto 5 winning rows

lines: Count the win-rows — that's the trap the table is setting

beats.narration_text: Pull back to the price row. One model costs twice the other. The table's implicit argument: more wins justify the premium. Two inferences want to happen right now. Neither is safe.

manim.spec: same table as B02 with win circles; price row fades in at bottom with terracotta bracket

lines: More wins, twice the price — neither inference is safe yet

beats.narration_text: The naïve reads: count the win-rows, accept the implied price-to-performance ratio. Both are tempting. Both are how the table gets you. Neither is the analysis the table is dressed to look like.

The scoreboard the table invites: five wins, three losses, one tie. Laid flat it looks decisive. But a scoreboard is only as good as what's inside each cell — and three of those cells have contamination problems.

manim.spec: isotype tally grid: 5 terracotta circles (wins) / 3 ghost circles (losses) / 1 ink circle (tie), labeled W-L-T, caption 'the invited scoreboard'; then terracotta ring draws around three of the win circles with label 'contamination?'

production_viz.label: 5-3-1 win tally with contamination query
production_viz.mechanic: isotype grid of colored circles builds row by row; ring draws on 3 wins
production_viz.note: qualitative — no real benchmark numbers appear

lines: 5 wins / 3 losses / 1 tie — the scoreboard the table invites
But what's actually inside those cells?

beats.narration_text: A comparison table is a rhetorical object, not a neutral one. It chose its rows, framed its columns, and ordered its metrics. Every choice was a judgment call. Understanding how it fools you is more durable than trusting its numbers.

lines: A comparison table is a rhetorical object.
It chose its rows — framed its columns — ordered its metrics.
Every choice was a judgment call. None of it is neutral.

beats.act: ACT II — Trap 1: The Headline Isn't Pure
beats.narration_text: Trap one. The headline isn't pure.

lines: Trap 1 — The Headline Isn't Pure

beats.narration_text: The headline column shows the higher of two variants — a safeguarded public model versus an unrestricted twin trained on the same base. These are different products. Merging their best results into one column means the number you're reading doesn't describe anything you can actually buy.

lines: The headline column shows the higher of two variants:
a safeguarded public model vs its unrestricted twin.
Merged into one column — the number isn't a product. It's a construction.

beats.narration_text: Look at the glossy launch chart. A ring draws around one starred row. The footnote says which variant scored here. That footnote is the contamination tell — the row was scored by the product you didn't price.

manim.spec: illustrative bar chart; star on one bar; terracotta ring draws; footnote '† unrestricted variant scored this row' fades in; caption (illustrative)

lines: The footnote is the contamination tell — read it before trusting the row

beats.narration_text: The footnote: this row is the other variant. A column that takes the better of two non-interchangeable variants isn't measuring a product. It's constructing an argument. The argument is dressed as a measurement.

manim.spec: two-row table header: 'THE CHEAPER MODEL' and 'THE PREMIUM MODEL'; a starred cell in the premium column; then footnote text fades in '† = unrestricted variant'; terracotta underline draws under the starred cell; SerifLabel below: 'this cell ≠ the product you priced'

production_viz.label: footnote reveal showing variant contamination
production_viz.mechanic: state card: table header → starred cell → footnote fade → terracotta underline draw
production_viz.note: no real model names; starred symbol is the visual anchor

lines: † = the other variant
This column isn't a product. It's a construction.

beats.narration_text: Generalize the trap: any column that takes the better of two non-interchangeable variants isn't describing a product. Before you count a win, ask which variant scored it — and whether that variant is the one you can deploy.

items.label: Which variant scored this row?
items.sub: safeguarded vs unrestricted — they're different products

items.label: Is that variant the one you can deploy?
items.sub: a win you can't buy is not a win

beats.narration_text: Trap two. You're not scoring a model — you're scoring a system.

lines: Trap 2 — You're Scoring a System

beats.narration_text: The routing diagram: a flagged prompt reroutes to a fallback — often a different model entirely. The 'model' column in the benchmark wraps a routing layer, a safety filter, and a fallback path. What was scored isn't the model. It's the system.

manim.spec: flow: prompt→router→safety filter→model→fallback; ACC curved reroute arrow when flagged; caption 'the model column wraps all of this'

lines: Prompt → router → safety filter → model → fallback (if flagged)
The 'model' column wraps all of this.
What was scored is the system — not just the model.

beats.narration_text: Server racks. Slow push in. A production inference system is not a single model call — it's a stack: routers, safety filters, fallback paths. Every component in that stack has a policy. Those policies were inside the benchmark.

manim.spec: vertical stack: prompt→router→safety filter→model→fallback; boxes build top-to-bottom with arrows; caption 'every component has a policy'

lines: Every component in the inference stack has a policy — and they're all in the score

beats.narration_text: Pan to one lit node. Part of the score came from here — not from the model under test. The benchmark couldn't control for the harness because the harness isn't fixed. It changes by deployment surface and by date.

manim.spec: same inference stack; fallback box highlighted ACC with ring; note 'part of the score came from here'

lines: Part of the score came from here — not from the model under test

beats.narration_text: The equation: score is a function of the model, the harness, and the fallback rate. Watch the harness term light up. In a production benchmark, that term can be larger than the model term. The model column is understating its own complexity.

manim.spec: three-term equation builds: 'score' = 'f(model' + ', harness' + ', fallback)'; each term appears one at a time; then the harness term and fallback term recolor to terracotta and enlarge; SerifLabel: 'the model column hides these two terms'

production_viz.label: score equation with harness term highlighted
production_viz.mechanic: sequential term reveal, terracotta accent on harness+fallback
production_viz.note: qualitative; no numbers; ink for model term, terracotta for harness+fallback

lines: score = f(model, harness, fallback)
The harness term is as large as — or larger than — the model term

beats.narration_text: The reroute rules in your deployment are different from the ones in the benchmark. The model you score in the test is not the model you run in production. The gap between them is the harness — and the harness is yours to configure.

lines: Benchmark harness ≠ your production harness.
The model you tested is not the model you'll run.
The gap is yours to configure — and yours to own.

beats.narration_text: Trap three. The compute budgets were not matched.

lines: Trap 3 — Unmatched Effort

beats.narration_text: Two dials at different settings. The premium model ran at extended thinking, high effort. The cheaper model ran at default. You are not comparing models — you are comparing models at different clock speeds. That is not a race. That is a setup.

manim.spec: two circular dial gauges side by side; left dial labeled 'the premium model' pointer near MAX; right dial labeled 'the cheaper model' pointer near MIN; terracotta label between them: 'not the same race'; caption below: '(illustrative effort levels)'

production_viz.label: two dials at different effort settings
production_viz.mechanic: dial gauges animate needles to HIGH vs DEFAULT positions
production_viz.note: qualitative; no actual token/compute numbers; illustrative

lines: The premium model: extended thinking. The cheaper model: default.
Different effort levels. This isn't a race — it's a setup.

beats.narration_text: The non-monotonic curve: score rises with compute budget, then dips, then rises again. The same model at different effort settings produces meaningfully different scores. An effort-unmatched comparison can produce almost any ranking you want — by choosing the effort levels for each model.

manim.spec: axes: x = 'compute budget (relative)', y = 'score'; a curve draws that rises, dips, then rises again (non-monotonic S-shape); terracotta dot placed at an arbitrary point on the dip; SerifLabel: 'where you measure determines the winner'; caption bottom: '(qualitative — illustrative)'

production_viz.label: non-monotonic score vs compute curve
production_viz.mechanic: animated curve draw; terracotta dot marks a measurement choice
production_viz.note: strictly qualitative; shape is the argument; no real benchmark numbers

lines: Score vs compute is non-monotonic.
Where you measure determines the winner — not the model.

beats.narration_text: The honest label in this source is UNKNOWN effort — which is what it said. An unlabeled effort column is the warning sign. Treat every row in a table with no effort column as a configuration choice presented as a model measurement.

lines: The honest label is: UNKNOWN effort.
An unlabeled effort column means: the author chose for you.
Treat it as a configuration choice, not a model measurement.

beats.narration_text: A technical spec sheet. A ring draws around the effort field — it's blank. The blank isn't an omission. It's an argument: we chose the effort level that produced this result, and we'd prefer you not ask why.

manim.spec: drawn spec form; 5 rows; Effort row has blank dashed value; terracotta ring draws around it; label 'Effort: ——'

lines: The blank effort field is not an omission — it's an argument

beats.act: ACT V — The Reframe: Price Isn't Cost
beats.narration_text: The reframe. Price isn't cost — and that changes everything.

lines: The Reframe — Price Isn't Cost

beats.narration_text: Per-token price tag versus per-task receipt. These are different numbers. The price tag is what the provider charges per input token. The receipt is what a task actually costs: price times token count, divided by the fraction that succeed, times the retry multiplier.

lines: The price tag: dollars per token.
The receipt: (price × tokens) ÷ pass-rate × (1 + retries).
These are different numbers — sometimes very different numbers.

beats.narration_text: Build the formula: cost per completed task equals price per token times tokens used, divided by pass rate, times the retry multiplier. When the cheaper model's pass rate is low enough, its per-task cost exceeds the premium model's. The per-token price is not the cost.

manim.spec: equation builds term by term: 'cost/task' → '= (price/token × tokens)' → '÷ pass_rate' → '× (1 + retry_rate)'; each term appears with a brief pause; pass_rate term pulses terracotta; SerifLabel under pass_rate: 'this term can flip the ranking'

production_viz.label: cost-per-task formula with pass rate highlighted
production_viz.mechanic: sequential term build; terracotta pulse on pass_rate denominator
production_viz.note: qualitative formula only; no actual prices or pass rates — mechanism not measurement

lines: cost/task = (price/token × tokens) ÷ pass_rate × (1 + retries)
The pass-rate denominator can flip the ranking entirely

beats.narration_text: Illustrative bars. Cheaper per token, higher pass rate — the per-task receipt is lower. Premium per token, lower pass rate — the receipt is higher. The direction reverses depending on where you land on the pass-rate axis. This is the normal regime for long-context tasks.

manim.spec: two-scenario bar chart; scenario A: 'cheaper model' shorter bar (lower cost/task); scenario B: 'premium model' shorter bar (lower cost/task); flip animation shows the bars swapping positions with a direction arrow; caption: '(illustrative — not real measurements)'; both bars labeled with generics not specifics

production_viz.label: illustrative cost bars showing ranking reversal
production_viz.mechanic: two bars animate; swap direction arrows; illustrative caption
production_viz.note: strictly qualitative; labeled ILLUSTRATIVE on screen; no real numbers

lines: (illustrative)
The per-token winner can be the per-task loser — depending on pass rate.

beats.narration_text: A long itemized receipt beside a single price sticker. The sticker shows one number. The receipt shows token count, retry count, verbosity charges, re-run costs. The gap between the two is where the cheaper model stops being cheap.

manim.spec: left: price tag box; right: itemized receipt building line by line (input tokens/retries/verbosity/re-run); total line; caption (illustrative)

lines: The sticker and the receipt are very different documents

beats.narration_text: Pan down the receipt. Retries add up. Verbosity charges tokens. Re-runs cost full price. A model that produces fewer retries is cheaper per task even if its token rate is higher. The price tag never told you that.

manim.spec: receipt lines all visible; each ACC-highlights in sequence as narration names retries/verbosity/re-runs; total line; caption (illustrative)

lines: Retries. Verbosity. Re-runs. The receipt builds while the sticker stayed fixed.

beats.act: the per-token winner can be the per-task loser
beats.narration_text: The flip: the per-token winner can be the per-task loser. The table's price row is not the cost row. If you're buying capability at scale, the table's most prominent number may be its least useful one.

lines: Per-token winner ≠ per-task winner.
The price row is not the cost row.
At scale, the table's most prominent number may be its least useful one.

beats.narration_text: The trap capability can't fix. Some constraints aren't capability problems.

lines: The Trap Capability Can't Fix

beats.narration_text: A funnel. At the top: the full set of models. A compliance filter narrows it — data retention policy, output certification, privacy architecture. The models that survive are the only ones in the race. Capability enters the analysis only after the filter, not before.

manim.spec: funnel: wide top 'All models' → ACC filter band 'Compliance filter' → narrow bottom 'Deployable subset'; arrow + label 'capability analysis starts here'

lines: All models → compliance filter → deployable subset.
Capability analysis starts at the bottom of the funnel.
A model blocked at the top has a benchmark lead of zero.

beats.narration_text: A locked records room. A redacted compliance page. For regulated sectors, the compliance gate isn't a preference — it's binary. You can deploy this model or you cannot. If you cannot, its benchmark lead is exactly zero.

manim.spec: binary split: CAN DEPLOY (INK left) vs CANNOT DEPLOY (ACC right); 'benchmark lead = 0' below right box

lines: Can you deploy it? If no — the benchmark lead is zero.

beats.narration_text: The gate assembled: can you deploy it? If no — benchmark lead is zero. If yes — capability analysis begins. The comparison table skipped the gate. That's not a gap you can fix by re-reading the table.

manim.spec: diamond decision node: 'Can you deploy it?'; YES branch → ink arrow to 'capability analysis'; NO branch → terracotta arrow to 'benchmark lead = 0'; the NO branch draws last and the '= 0' term writes in terracotta

production_viz.label: binary compliance gate decision diagram
production_viz.mechanic: decision diamond → YES/NO branches; NO branch in terracotta
production_viz.note: simple flow diagram; terracotta on the zero result

lines: Can you deploy it? No → benchmark lead = 0.
The table skipped this gate entirely.

beats.act: ACT VII — How to Trust the Analysis
beats.narration_text: How to trust the analysis. Look for its seams.

lines: How to Trust the Analysis

beats.act: the analysis that shows its seams
beats.narration_text: The analysis that earns trust shows evidence against its own conclusion, a section it can't resolve, and its own UNKNOWN labels. A seamless table — all wins, clean columns, no footnotes — is not evidence of quality. It is evidence that the author hid the seams.

items.label: Shows disconfirming evidence
items.sub: evidence against the conclusion is included

items.label: Labels its own unknowns
items.sub: UNKNOWN is honest, not a weakness

beats.narration_text: The checklist assembles: is the headline column pure? Is the score from a system or a model? Is effort matched? What is the cost per completed task, not per token? Does a compliance constraint eliminate a model before capability matters? Five checks. That is the lens.

manim.spec: five checklist rows appear one by one with a checkmark icon; labels: '1. Headline purity' / '2. System score?' / '3. Effort matched?' / '4. Cost per task, not per token' / '5. Compliance gate first'; each row fades in sequentially; on completion all five rows collectively recolor to terracotta accent; SerifLabel 'the reusable lens' appears below

production_viz.label: five-check lens checklist builds row by row
production_viz.mechanic: sequential checklist rows; collective terracotta accent on completion
production_viz.note: text only — no benchmark numbers; mechanism not measurement

lines: 1. Headline purity  2. System score  3. Effort matched
4. Per-task cost  5. Compliance gate first
Five checks — the reusable lens

beats.narration_text: Distrust the seamless table. Trust the one that labels what it doesn't know. A source that names its own unknowns is doing the work the reader can't — and that's the only version of the analysis worth handing to a decision.

lines: Distrust the seamless table.
Trust the one that labels what it doesn't know.
A source that names its unknowns is doing the work the reader can't.

beats.narration_text: The reusable lens. Headline purity — ask which variant scored that row. System score — the harness is inside the number. Effort match — unmatched compute is not a fair race. Per-task cost — the token price is not the bill. Compliance gate — if you can't deploy it, its benchmark lead is zero. Five checks. That is the table you were always reading.

artifactLines: 1. Headline purity — which variant scored this row?
2. System score — the harness is inside the number
3. Effort matched — unmatched compute is not a race
4. Per-task cost — the token price is not the bill
5. Compliance gate — before capability matters at all

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Point this at any model-comparison table and run the five checks out loud. Which rows blend variants? Which scores came from a harness, not the model alone? Is effort matched? What does the cost per completed task look like — not per token? And before any of that: does a compliance constraint eliminate a model without the table mentioning it?

props.command: Take any model comparison table. Apply the five-check skeptic's lens: headline purity → system score → effort match → per-task cost → compliance gate. What do you find?
props.runningText: your turn — run the five checks…

beats.narration_text: Two Models, Twice the Price. Liam, in for Bear.
